extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness of design patent claims under 35 U.S.C. 103, including scope of prior art, prima facie analysis, combining references, and consideration of secondary (objective) evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the Prior Art (Analogous Arts)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of the relevant prior art for purposes of evaluating obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 extends to all 'analogous arts.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use In re Glavas guidance for design context: 'The question in design cases is not whether the references sought to be combined are in analogous arts in the mechanical sense, but whether they are so related that the appearance of certain ornamental features in one would suggest the application of those features to the other.' If the problem is merely one of giving an attractive appearance to a surface, it is immaterial whether the surface is wallpaper, an oven door, or crockery. Where differences are in shape or form, the nature of the articles must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of Differences Between Claimed Design and Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: All differences between the claimed design and the closest prior art reference should be identified in any rejection of the design claim under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mere fact that there are differences is not alone sufficient to justify patentability (see In re Lamb). If any differences are considered de minimis or inconsequential from a design viewpoint, the rejection should so state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of Ordinary Skill in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness must be evaluated from the perspective of a 'designer of . . . articles of the types presented' — i.e., a designer of ordinary skill in the art to which the subject matter pertains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Nalbandian and In re Carter. Examiners must determine whether the design would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill with the claimed type of article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective Evidence of Nonobviousness (Secondary Considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations, such as commercial success and copying of the design by others, are relevant to the evaluation of obviousness of a design claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence may be presented at the time a prima facie case is evaluated or in rebuttal. Examiners must consider affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, evaluate nexus between success and the ornamental features, and follow MPEP § 716 et seq. See MRC Innovations v. Hunter, Crocs v. ITC, Litton System v. Whirlpool, and Avia Group v. L.A. Gear for principles on evaluation and nexus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima Facie Obviousness — Overall Appearance Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103, it is the overall appearance of the design that must be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After factual inquiries (Graham v. John Deere), examiner must determine whether they establish a prima facie case. To establish prima facie obviousness, all claim limitations must be taught or suggested by the prior art. The proper standard is whether the design would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill with the claimed type of article (see In re Nalbandian).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary Reference Must Provide Substantially the Same Overall Appearance
rubrics_metrics.description: A primary reference must be more than a design concept; it must have an appearance substantially the same as the claimed design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design characteristics = overall visual appearance. If no primary reference with substantially the same overall appearance exists, no holding of obviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103 can be made, whether based on a single reference alone or in view of modifications suggested by secondary prior art (see In re Rosen, In re Harvey, Yardley, Leslie).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining References — Suggestion to Modify (Motivation to Combine)
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103 is appropriate if a designer of ordinary skill would have been motivated to modify a primary reference by deleting features or by interchanging with or adding features from pertinent secondary references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be some suggestion in the prior art to modify the basic design with features from the secondary references (see In re Borden). The long-standing test: whether references are so related that appearance of certain ornamental features in one would suggest application to the other (In re Glavas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition Against Destroying the Broad Function When Combining References
rubrics_metrics.description: If the proposed combination of references so alters the primary reference that its broad function can no longer be carried out, the combination would not have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is permissible to modify the primary reference to the extent the specific function may be affected while the broad function remains. Example: modifying an 'airtight' cabinet so it is no longer airtight is permissible if it still functions as a cabinet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous Art Requirement When Modifying Configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: When a modification to a primary reference involves a change in configuration, both the primary and secondary references must be from analogous arts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply In re Glavas: configuration changes require analogous-art secondary references; analogous art may be more broadly interpreted for simulative portions of a design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface Ornamentation Exception for Analogous Art
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the differences are limited to the application of ornamentation to the surface of an article, any prior art reference which discloses substantially the same surface ornamentation would be considered analogous art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When modifying the surface to provide an attractive appearance, it is immaterial whether the secondary reference is analogous art since the modification does not involve a change in configuration or structure and would not have destroyed the characteristics of the primary reference (see In re Glavas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional or Hidden Features Cannot Support Patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Features of the design which are functional and/or hidden during end use may not be relied upon to support patentability; a design claim must be ornamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must provide evidence to support the prima facie functionality of such features. Hidden portions or functional features cannot be relied upon as a basis for patentability. If applicant wishes to rely on functional/hidden features, the standard for establishing ornamentality under 35 U.S.C. 171 must be applied (see Jones v. Progress Ind., In re Cornwall, In re Garbo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — Evidence Must Be Considered (Burden Shift)
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a prima facie case of obviousness has been established, the burden shifts to the applicant to rebut it, if possible, with objective evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All rebuttal evidence submitted by applicant, including affidavits or declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, must be considered by examiners in determining patentability under 35 U.S.C. 103. See MPEP § 716–716.06 for additional guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — Teaching Away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness can be rebutted if the applicant can show that the art in any material respect 'taught away' from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference teaches away when a person of ordinary skill, upon reading the reference, would be led in a direction divergent from the path taken by the applicant (see In re Haruna).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of Commercial Success Evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: When evidence of commercial success is submitted, examiners must evaluate whether there is objective evidence of success and whether the success can be attributed to the ornamental design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affidavit or declaration under 37 CFR 1.132 has minimal evidentiary value on commercial success without nexus showing connection between sales and ornamental features. See Litton System v. Whirlpool and Avia Group v. L.A. Gear; consult MPEP § 716.01(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for Expert Testimony in Rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Submission of expert testimony must establish the professional credentials of the person signing the affidavit or declaration and should not express an opinion on the ultimate legal issue of obviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert statements should avoid concluding legal questions (obviousness is a question of law). See Avia Group Int’l Inc. v. L.A. Gear and Panduit Corp. v. Dennison Mfg. Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for Copying Evidence in Rebuttal
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that competitors are copying the design may be relevant, but more than mere copying is necessary to make it significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Copying may be attributable to other factors (lack of concern for patents or indifference to enforcement). Examiners should assess whether copying reflects recognition of the ornamental design (see Cable Electric Products v. Genmark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'Something in Existence' / Design Characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A design must be compared with 'something in existence,' defined as 'a reference... the design characteristics of which are basically the same as the claimed design.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This means overall visual appearance; a primary reference that does not give the same visual impression (different overall appearance/aesthetic appeal) is not sufficient (see In re Jennings, In re Rosen, In re Harvey, Yardley, Leslie).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural Form Paragraphs and Remedies to Overcome 103 Rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraphs provide language for rejections and list procedural showings that may overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection (single or multiple references; AIA/pre-AIA differences; common ownership; provisional rejections).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possible ways to overcome a rejection include: (1) showing under 37 CFR 1.130(a) that the design in the reference was obtained from the inventor (not prior art); (2) perfecting a claim to priority under 35 U.S.C. 119 by filing certified priority documents satisfying 35 U.S.C. 112(a); (3) perfecting benefit claim under 35 U.S.C. 120 with an application data sheet under 37 CFR 1.76 and establishing enablement/description under 35 U.S.C. 112(a); (4) showing prior public disclosure under 37 CFR 1.130(b); (5) providing a statement under 35 U.S.C. 102(b)(2)(C) of common ownership/assignment; (6) merging applications or showing common ownership to overcome provisional rejections. Examiner Notes describe bracket insertion and sequencing requirements (e.g., preceding form paragraphs for certain priority situations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous Art for Simulative Portions of a Design
rubrics_metrics.description: Analogous art can be more broadly interpreted when a claim is directed to a design with a portion simulating a well-known or naturally occurring object or person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The simulative nature of that portion of the design is prima facie evidence that art which simulates that portion would be within the level of ordinary skill under 35 U.S.C. 103.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Secondary References Must Leave No Doubt
rubrics_metrics.description: If differences between the claimed design and a primary reference are shown by secondary references, they should be applied so as to leave no doubt that those differences would have been obvious to a designer of ordinary skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should ensure that application of secondary references demonstrates that the differences are minor/unrelated to overall aesthetic appearance or that the combination would have been obvious (see In re Nalbandian, In re Sapp).
